pages.text: # Busting the attention span myth A group of people holding their mobile phones You probably won't get to the end of this article. Everyone knows our attention spans are getting shorter. It's just obvious. Or is it? In the always-connected world of social media, smartphones and hyperlinks, external in the middle of everything you read, it can feel that much harder to stay focused. And there are statistics too. They say that the average attention span is down from 12 seconds in the year 2000 to eight seconds now. That is less than the nine-second attention span of your average goldfish. [...] As if to prove it, the number-lovers at Statistic Brain source all their figures. But the sources are infuriatingly vague. And when I contact the listed sources - the National Center for Biotechnology Information at the US National Library of Medicine, and the Associated Press - neither can find any record of research that backs up the stats. My attempts to contact Statistic Brain came to nothing too. I have spoken to various people who dedicate their working lives to studying human attention and they have no idea where the numbers come from either. ## 'Task-dependent' In fact, they think the idea that attention spans are getting shorter is plain wrong. "I don't think that's true at all," says Dr Gemma Briggs, a psychology lecturer at the Open University.

judgment.evidence: BBC reporter contacted the listed sources and interviewed attention researchers; the Time link is only a reference to the claim.

pages.primaryEvidenceReason: Firsthand reporting: the sources named for the statistic could find no supporting research.

pages.title: Are attention spans really shrinking? What the science says | Scientific American
pages.publishedDateEvidence: Publisher's schema.org datePublished (JSON-LD), read from the page itself
pages.text: Often included in discussion of these results is a 2015 marketing report by Microsoft Canada, which stated that the average human attention span had fallen from 12 seconds in 2000 to 8 seconds in 2013. The report noted that this was shorter than a goldfish’s average attention span, which it reported as 9 seconds. But the report’s findings, based on surveys, filmed behaviour and electroencephalogram (EEG) data — which uses spikes in brain activity to measure when people switch their focus — reflected changing digital habits rather than cognitive limits and even noted that people were becoming more efficient at processing information. (Also, goldfish are unfairly maligned; there is no evidence that they have particularly short attention spans, and studies show they retain some information [...] The idea of an average attention span carries intuitive appeal. But the way it’s discussed can tangle distinct concepts. Researchers distinguish between people’s capacity to pay attention, that is, their underlying ability to concentrate on a particular task, and their real-world behaviour, or what people actually focus on from moment to moment. What’s more, the capacity to pay attention is the result of several processes in the brain. These include sustained attention, the ability to stay engaged with a task over time; selective attention, the ability to prioritize some information and ignore the rest; and executive control, the ability to steer attention in line with a goal rather than whatever happens to be more tempting. ## Attention in the laboratory

pages.title: Eight seconds and dropping? How to make the most of short attention spans
pages.publishedDateEvidence: Publisher's published <time> element, read from the page itself
pages.text: We are regularly bombarded with information about a steep drop in attention spans. Based on its own data in 2015, Microsoft reported that the average attention span had dropped from about 12 seconds for millennials to eight seconds for gen Z. That survey has been widely debunked, but the question of whether attention spans are getting shorter remains. And as the new Premier League season kicked off, UEFA introduced a new “eight seconds rule” stating a goalkeeper cannot hold the ball for more than eight seconds or the opposing team wins a corner kick. Coincidence? The rule was introduced to avoid time wasting. It may be that the mean length of attention needed to kick the ball is on average eight seconds. And perhaps this is also how long viewers can pay attention when nothing’s happening. [...] Editor’s note: This article was updated on September 30 to show that the claim Microsoft made about the average attention span dropping from about 12 seconds for millennials to eight seconds for gen Z was unsubstantiated.

pages.title: Attention Span: The 8-Second Goldfish Myth | IQ Metrics
pages.publishedDateEvidence: Publisher's schema.org datePublished (JSON-LD), read from the page itself
pages.text: ## What you need to know No. The claim that the average human attention span is 8 seconds, shorter than the attention span of a goldfish, has no study behind it. It sits on one slide of a 2015 Microsoft Canada report, which gives the goldfish 9 seconds and credits a website called Statistic Brain. The BBC found that neither source Statistic Brain listed could confirm the numbers. Researchers it spoke to said an average attention span is meaningless, because attention depends on the task. Below: where the 8-second figure came from, what the Microsoft report did measure, what we know about goldfish, one peer-reviewed measure of how long workers stay on a screen, and whether attention spans are shrinking. We opened the BBC article and the Microsoft report themselves on 12 November 2026. [...] ## Is the average human attention span 8 seconds? The human attention span 8 seconds figure is not a measured result. The figure appears once in Microsoft Canada's Consumer Insights report Attention Spans (Spring 2015), on a slide headed "We know human attention is dwindling", with the source line "Statistic brain". The slide lists the average human attention span as 12 seconds in 2000 and 8 seconds in 2013, and the average attention span of a goldfish as 9 seconds.

judgment.evidence: States it opened the Microsoft report itself and traces the slide and sources, in addition to relying on the BBC findings.

pages.primaryEvidenceReason: Inspected the original Microsoft slide and its source line directly.

Additional studies suggest that the average attention span for adults is around 8 seconds, with some researchers even proposing it could be as short as 2.8 seconds in today's digital era. pages.title: Is Your Attention Span Shorter Than a Goldfish's? Where the Claim Came From and What Helps You Focus
pages.publishedDateEvidence: Publisher's article:published_time meta tag, read from the page itself
pages.text: How sure: Moderate the trail ends at a website whose listed sources found no research; a search cannot prove none exists. The claim says the average attention span fell from 12 seconds in 2000 to 8, less than a goldfish’s 9. It had appeared in newspapers, magazines, on radio and in a management book. The BBC statistics programme More or Less traced it in 2017. The figure led back to a 2015 industry report, which credited it to another website. The sources that website listed could find no research behind it. The report itself shows the hand-off. In it, the three figures sit under the heading “We know human attention is dwindling”, credited in one line to the statistics website. It gives 8 seconds as the average for 2013. [...] The report’s own research measured something else. It surveyed 2,000 Canadians and studied the brain activity of 112 people. It split attention into three kinds, because “we don’t think that attention can be simply characterized as how long people can concentrate”. We followed the credit back one more step. The earliest archived copy of the website’s page that we found, from February 2012, already lists the three figures. There, 8 seconds is the average for 2012. By 2015 the same line said 2013. The only study the page names sits under its web-browsing figures, not under the attention-span lines. That is where the trail stops. We found no earlier copy, and no study that measured these numbers.

judgment.evidence: Traces the claim through the Microsoft report to an archived 2012 Statistic Brain page, going beyond the BBC link.

analysis.answer: The claim that average human attention span is 8 seconds (down from 12 in 2000, and shorter than a goldfish's 9) is not backed by identifiable research; the BBC found the cited sources could not find any research supporting the statistics [1]. The 8-second figure appears on a single slide of a 2015 Microsoft Canada report, which credited the website Statistic Brain, and it is not a measured result [2] [3]. Researchers say an average attention span is not meaningful, because attention depends on the task [2]. The Microsoft report's own research (surveys and EEG) measured different things, such as changing digital habits, rather than establishing a general 8-second attention span limit [3].
